digest.definition: Engineering creates, develops and applies technology, processes and systems that improve lives and protect people, joining ingenuity and creativity to science and mathematics; at its core is putting things together and designing things that work, and then work better
distinctiveFeatures: Engineering creates, develops and applies technology, processes and systems that improve lives and protect people, joining ingenuity and creativity to science and mathematics; at its core is putting things together and designing things that work, and then work better
It aims at fair and sustainable answers to global challenges, read through the UN Sustainable Development Goals and through cybersecurity, infrastructure, manufacturing, mobility and energy

It is a very broad subject of many disciplines and specialisms, studied as the BEng with honours, the integrated MEng and the taught MSc, with general and multidisciplinary courses beside single-specialism ones
Study usually covers five areas: scientific and mathematical principles; analysis with computational tools; design, creativity and innovation; engineering and society; and engineering practice
Problem-solving runs from broadly defined, single-domain problems to complex problems with no obvious or optimal answer, met early in the course
Practical work, physical or software build-and-test, sets it apart from other applied sciences
Ethics, safety and security are core professional concerns, each with its own section
It is shaped by the profession: most degrees are accredited by professional engineering institutions licensed by the Engineering Council against AHEP, and industry is involved in design and delivery

themesInSubject.inThisSubject: a more diverse profession and equitable designs for users worldwide; EDI embedded from team make-up to solutions; global perspectives and the questioning of historic western assumptions; inclusive course culture and fair assessment of group work (D1, 1.13 to 1.15, 2.4, 2.14, 3.14)

accessible design as a standard part of the curriculum; accessible labs, workshops, group work and placements, hidden disabilities included; flexible delivery and reasonable adjustments in assessment (D1, 1.16 to 1.18, 3.13, 3.14)

headed Sustainability: engineers as builders of a sustainable future; the SDGs encouraged in design, teaching and assessment; lifecycle and resource impact; challenging industry norms for net zero (D1, 1.2, 1.19, 1.20, 2.3, 2.13)

standards.rungBases: Three awards, each with the same three rungs under its own headings. Threshold: a list of five outcome categories, mapped onto a third (honours and MEng) or a pass (MSc), with the threshold also set by the accrediting institution where the course is accredited (4.8, 4.11, 4.15); for accredited courses AHEP's outcomes are the threshold (4.5). Typical (2:1 and 2:2; merit) and excellent (first; distinction) state no outcomes: their criteria follow each provider's marking scheme (4.9, 4.10, 4.12, 4.13, 4.16, 4.17); for honours, 4.6 points to Annex D. Each typical and excellent paragraph is held as one record.

subjectSpecific.text: When you graduate, you will be able to show that you have met the standards for your degree; your course publishes its outcomes and assesses you against them.

headingPath: Context and purpose of an Engineering degree

statements.appliesTo: engineers in training and in practice
statements.about: adaptable engineers and a changing curriculum
statements.paraphrase: Engineering innovation is key to fair and sustainable answers to the world's hardest problems, read through the UN Sustainable Development Goals and challenges such as cybersecurity, energy and mobility; future engineers must be able to adapt as new challenges appear, so the curriculum keeps changing.

forPractitioner.text: Prepare students to adapt to new and emerging challenges, since future engineers must be adaptable; use the UN Sustainable Development Goals and global challenges such as energy, infrastructure and cybersecurity as reference points, and expect the curriculum to keep changing.

forBeneficiary.text: As a future engineer you must be ready to adapt to new challenges as they arise, from climate and sustainable development to cybersecurity, energy and transport.

headingPath: Context and purpose of an Engineering degree

statements.about: making honours and non-honours bachelor's titles clear
statements.paraphrase: An honours bachelor's degree is a first-cycle award, usually three years full time (four in Scotland), with 90 or more credits at FHEQ Level 6 (SCQF Level 10); a non-honours bachelor's carries less credit and meets the level only in part. Because everyday usage drops 'honours' or 'ordinary', providers should remove the confusion by saying what each title means in their course information.

forPractitioner.text: State plainly in course information for applicants and employers what each bachelor's title means, honours or not, since everyday usage blurs the two; this is a should, aimed at the provider.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the provider to explain award titles; the student meets its effect in course information

headingPath: Context and purpose of an Engineering degree

statements.about: solving broadly defined and complex problems
statements.paraphrase: Depending on the course, students will build skill either in solving broadly defined problems within one domain or in tackling increasingly complex, integrated sociotechnical systems; broadly defined problems call for sensible assumptions and balanced requirements, while complex problems lack an obvious or optimal answer and demand creativity. Learners will need early exposure to problems so they get enough practice.

forPractitioner.text: Plan for students to meet engineering problems from the first stage and to progress, according to the course, either to broadly defined single-domain problems or to complex integrated systems with no obvious best answer; students will develop the knowledge, confidence and skill to handle them.

forBeneficiary.text: You will build your skill at solving engineering problems, starting early in your studies: either well-defined problems in one area, or increasingly complex problems that mix technical and social factors and have no single obvious answer.

headingPath: Context and purpose of an Engineering degree

statements.about: EDI embedded in engineering practice and curricula
statements.paraphrase: Equality, diversity and inclusion belong in every part of engineering, from the make-up of the team through the process to the solutions society receives, and should be built into all activity; where projects design for developing or international settings, it matters greatly that students grasp the technical and wider context and include cultural and user views, so curricula should build global perspectives and help students recognise inherited western assumptions.

forPractitioner.text: Embed equality, diversity and inclusion throughout the course, from team composition to the design process and its outcomes; in projects for developing or international contexts, make sure students understand the whole setting and bring in cultural and user perspectives. The curriculum should foster global perspectives and help students see historic western assumptions.

forBeneficiary.text: You should see equality, diversity and inclusion as part of all engineering work, from who is on the team to what you design; when you design for other countries or cultures, it is vital that you understand the setting and include the views of the people who will use the solution.

headingPath: Context and purpose of an Engineering degree

statements.about: accessibility in access to and within the curriculum
statements.paraphrase: Accessibility advances EDI, and engineering can itself remove barriers in society, so accessibility should be weighed both in access to engineering education and inside the curriculum, which calls for flexible learning, teaching and assessment (see 3.13).

forPractitioner.text: Consider accessibility twice: in who can get into and through the course, and in what the curriculum teaches; flexible approaches to learning, teaching and assessment carry this out (3.13).

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the provider; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

headingPath: Context and purpose of an Engineering degree

statements.about: accessibility as standard in curricula and design
statements.paraphrase: Accessibility should be a normal part of engineering curricula, above all in design, so that solutions remove barriers and support inclusion; curricula should also be designed with accessibility in mind, at least meeting statutory requirements.

forPractitioner.text: Teach accessibility as a routine part of the curriculum, especially in design work, so students produce solutions that remove barriers; design the curriculum itself to be accessible, meeting legal requirements as the floor.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the provider; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

headingPath: Context and purpose of an Engineering degree

statements.about: removing barriers for disabled students
statements.paraphrase: Learning environments built with accessibility first can let disabled students study engineering who otherwise could not; accessibility measures should remove barriers to taking part, should reach past laboratories and workshops to every part of the curriculum including group work and placements, and should cover hidden disabilities so that no one is disadvantaged.

forPractitioner.text: Make accessibility a primary concern so disabled students can study engineering: remove barriers to engagement in labs and workshops and also in group work, placements and every other part of the course, including for hidden disabilities.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the provider; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

headingPath: Context and purpose of an Engineering degree

statements.about: equipping sustainable engineers
statements.paraphrase: Courses should motivate students to become more sustainable engineers, giving them the knowledge and skills to judge the environmental and social effects of solutions; using the UN Sustainable Development Goals in curriculum design, teaching and assessment is encouraged, including digital accessibility, resilience, adaptability and problem-solving.

forPractitioner.text: Equip students to weigh the environmental and social effects of engineering solutions, and draw on the UN Sustainable Development Goals in curriculum design, pedagogy and assessment (encouraged), including digital accessibility and resilience.

forBeneficiary.text: Your course should help you become a more sustainable engineer, able to weigh up the environmental and social effects of what you design.

headingPath: Context and purpose of an Engineering degree

statements.about: professional ethics and ethical judgement
statements.paraphrase: Engineers should work to the profession's ethical principles (the 2017 statement of the Engineering Council and Royal Academy of Engineering: honesty and integrity, respect for life, law, environment and public good, accuracy and rigour, leadership and communication) and should, through their studies, come to understand engineering's ethical issues and be able to judge and defend ethical choices; the Engineering Professors Council's toolkit supports teaching and assessing ethics.

forPractitioner.text: Teach students to work to the profession's ethical principles and assess their grasp of engineering's ethical issues and their ability to make and justify ethical judgements; the Engineering Ethics Toolkit offers case studies for embedding this.

forBeneficiary.text: You should learn to work by the profession's ethical principles, such as honesty, integrity and respect for life and the environment, and be able to make ethical judgements and explain why you made them.

headingPath: Context and purpose of an Engineering degree

statements.appliesTo: engineers in training and in practice
statements.about: protecting life: health and safety
statements.paraphrase: Protecting life is a central ethical concern, so engineers judge the health and safety of new and legacy solutions; they usually carry a daily responsibility for others' and their own well-being and need a detailed grasp of the legal frameworks and the skill to analyse and reduce hazards.

forPractitioner.text: Prepare students for the everyday responsibility of protecting others and themselves: teach the relevant legal frameworks in detail and build skill in hazard analysis and mitigation, for new and legacy solutions.

forBeneficiary.text: Engineers carry everyday responsibility for keeping people safe, so you need a detailed understanding of the safety laws that apply and the skills to analyse and reduce hazards.

headingPath: Context and purpose of an Engineering degree

statements.about: a holistic approach to safety
statements.paraphrase: Courses should help students build an all-round approach to safety across their studies, drawing on human behaviour, risk monitoring and management and the ability to specify and test such system qualities; students should understand the particular threats raised by growing automation and autonomy.

forPractitioner.text: Support students throughout the course to take a holistic view of safety: human behaviour, risk monitoring and management, and specifying and testing safety qualities; make sure they understand the new threats that automated and autonomous systems bring.

forBeneficiary.text: You should develop a rounded approach to safety, understanding how people behave, how risks are monitored and managed, and the new threats that come with automated and autonomous systems.

headingPath: Context and purpose of an Engineering degree

statements.about: safety as a non-functional system quality in design
statements.paraphrase: Complex systems are hard to develop because behaviour and interactions are unpredictable and political, socio-economic and environmental change shifts the risks; designers must still account for how people act with systems, and safety risks must be built explicitly into design approaches as non-functional attributes such as reliability, resilience, performance and usability, since failing them can breach legal duties; Engineering X offers teaching material.

forPractitioner.text: Teach design so that safety risks are explicitly included as non-functional system qualities (reliability, resilience, performance, usability), with attention to human behaviour and changing risk; failing to meet them can mean system failure and legal breach.

forBeneficiary.text: When you design a system, you must build in safety qualities such as reliability, resilience, performance and usability, and think about how people will really use it.

headingPath: Context and purpose of an Engineering degree

statements.about: security awareness and secure design
statements.paraphrase: Engineers know what security means and how deliberate hostile acts could affect their solutions; they can critically analyse the security consequences of their own design choices and work with others to build systems robust to threats, seeing the need to cover physical, people, process and technology aspects together.

forPractitioner.text: Graduates will be able to analyse critically the security consequences of their design decisions and collaborate to build threat-resistant systems, covering physical, human, process and technological aspects.

forBeneficiary.text: You will understand what security means in engineering, be able to judge how your own design choices affect it and work with others to make systems hard to attack.

headingPath: Context and purpose of an Engineering degree

statements.about: resolving security problems in legacy systems
statements.paraphrase: Learners gain context-specific knowledge of their branch of engineering; besides reducing security risks in new solutions, engineers can fix security weaknesses in existing systems, applying engineering thinking where data may be incomplete and changing designs to improve them.

forPractitioner.text: Develop students' contextual knowledge of their own branch so they will be able to resolve security problems in legacy systems as well as new ones, working with incomplete data and making design changes that improve things.

forBeneficiary.text: You will learn enough about your own branch of engineering to fix security problems in existing systems as well as new ones, even when you do not have all the data.

headingPath: Context and purpose of an Engineering degree

statements.about: safeguarding sensitive data
statements.paraphrase: Engineers often hold sensitive data, personal, defence or commercial, and have the knowledge and skill to protect it from security threats; they understand the importance of managing data, know the relevant legal frameworks and the ethical and legal side of sharing information, and can decide well about security-minded communication.

forPractitioner.text: Teach students to protect sensitive data (personal, defence, commercial), the legal frameworks that govern it, and the ethics and law of sharing information, so they will be able to make informed choices about secure communication.

forBeneficiary.text: You will know how to protect sensitive data, such as personal or commercial information, understand the laws that apply and make sound choices about sharing information securely.

headingPath: Context and purpose of an Engineering degree

statements.about: support for students on industrial placements
statements.paraphrase: Some students take placements or internships built into their degree; those who choose a formal industrial placement should get continued support from their institution so that they gain educationally as well as financially.

forPractitioner.text: Keep supporting students while they are on formal industrial placements, so the placement benefits their learning and not only their finances.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the institution to support placement students; the student receives the support

headingPath: Context and purpose of an Engineering degree

statements.about: accreditation for professional registration
statements.paraphrase: Engineers work across many professions, some of which need registration with a licensed institution; for a course to count towards a student's registration it must meet set requirements and standards and be accredited periodically, usually for up to five years, as AHEP explains.

forPractitioner.text: If the course is to count towards professional registration, it must meet the profession's requirements and be re-accredited periodically (usually at most every five years); consult the Engineering Council's AHEP.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a requirement on the course for accreditation; the student-facing effect is in 2.10 and 3.15

headingPath: Context and purpose of an Engineering degree

statements.about: the accreditation process and progression rules
statements.paraphrase: Accreditation in the UK is peer review by professional engineering institutions licensed by the Engineering Council, applied to single courses at named sites, checking that they give the grounding for registration as IEng or CEng; reviewers examine assessments, facilities and staffing so that every graduate meets the prescribed outcomes at the minimum threshold, and accredited courses also have to meet strict progression requirements so graduates have no gaps unfitting them for practice.

forPractitioner.text: For accredited courses, expect peer review of assessments, facilities and staffing against the prescribed outcomes at minimum threshold, and meet the stricter progression requirements accreditation imposes.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a requirement on accredited courses; the student meets its effect in progression rules (2.10, 3.15)

headingPath: Distinctive features of an Engineering degree

statements.about: readiness to start a professional career
statements.paraphrase: Engineering degrees are built to give graduates joined-up knowledge, skills and judgement that will let them start a professional career in engineering, and usually involve industry in their design and teaching.

forPractitioner.text: Design the degree so that graduates leave with integrated knowledge, skill and judgement that will let them begin professional engineering careers, involving industry in design and delivery.

forBeneficiary.text: Your degree is designed so that you will leave with the knowledge, skills and judgement to start a professional career in engineering.

headingPath: Distinctive features of an Engineering degree

statements.about: systems thinking and risk mitigation
statements.paraphrase: Engineering crosses technical and non-technical fields, so the degree readies graduates to think in systems and foresee system-level effects that reach into economic, political, legal, social, environmental and ethical matters; the curriculum should help engineers analyse and reduce risks to systems, above all to safety and security, so they can design against failure, cut bias and argue for social and environmental justice.

forPractitioner.text: Build systems thinking into the course and make sure the curriculum supports students in analysing and mitigating system risks, especially to safety and security, across economic, legal, social, environmental and ethical dimensions.

forBeneficiary.text: Your course should help you think about whole systems and analyse and reduce the risks they face, especially to safety and security, so you can design things that do not fail and treat people fairly.

headingPath: Distinctive features of an Engineering degree

statements.about: substantial practical and laboratory work
statements.paraphrase: To become rounded engineers, students are expected to have substantial practical experience, including hands-on laboratory and project work; learning by doing helps them grasp concepts and the logistics and health, safety and well-being sides of practical engineering.

forPractitioner.text: Give students substantial hands-on laboratory and project work so they develop rounded competence, understand concepts through experience and learn the practical logistics and health and safety of engineering.

forBeneficiary.text: You can expect a lot of hands-on lab and project work, which helps you understand ideas and learn how to work safely and practically.

headingPath: Distinctive features of an Engineering degree

statements.about: mathematical and scientific literacy
statements.paraphrase: Students should have enough opportunity to build the mathematical and scientific literacy their discipline or specialism needs.

forPractitioner.text: Provide enough chances for students to build the maths and science their discipline or specialism calls for.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course to offer opportunities; the student takes them up

headingPath: Distinctive features of an Engineering degree

statements.about: digital skills
statements.paraphrase: The curriculum should give students many chances to gain and improve digital skills that match society's needs in a more and more digital world.

forPractitioner.text: Offer plenty of opportunities across the curriculum for students to gain and extend digital skills that meet society's needs.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the curriculum to offer opportunities; the student takes them up

headingPath: Distinctive features of an Engineering degree

statements.about: autonomy, teamwork and leadership
statements.paraphrase: A mix of individual and supported group projects can build the self-directed learning, teamwork and leadership graduate work needs; students at higher FHEQ and FQHEIS levels are expected to learn more independently and to need less help in group work.

forPractitioner.text: Balance individual and facilitated group projects to build self-directed learning, teamwork and leadership; at higher levels, students will be expected to work more autonomously and need less facilitation in groups.

forBeneficiary.text: As you move up through the levels of your course, you will be expected to learn more independently and to need less help when working in groups.

headingPath: Distinctive features of an Engineering degree

statements.about: inclusive design and professional responsibility in projects
statements.paraphrase: Courses usually include design and research projects driven by industry and society; these should build in inclusive and accessible design and practice, and students ought to become able to balance economic, social and environmental needs and know their professional duties as engineers.

forPractitioner.text: Build inclusive and accessible design into design and research projects, and develop students' ability to balance economic, social and environmental needs with knowledge of their professional responsibilities.

forBeneficiary.text: In your projects you should learn to design inclusively and accessibly, balance economic, social and environmental needs, and understand your professional responsibilities as an engineer.

headingPath: Distinctive features of an Engineering degree

statements.about: managing compromise, complexity and missing information
statements.paraphrase: Uncertainty and competing factors are part of defining and solving engineering problems, so the degree gives graduates the ability to manage compromise; at higher FHEQ and FQHEIS levels students are expected to deal with more complex cases with more conflicting or missing information, and to reason critically to rational, justified decisions; applying this beyond design modules helps.

forPractitioner.text: Develop students' ability to manage compromise under uncertainty; at higher levels, students will be expected to handle more complex scenarios with conflicting or missing information and reach reasoned, justified decisions, ideally across modules and not only in design.

forBeneficiary.text: You will learn to handle trade-offs and uncertainty; as you progress you will be expected to deal with harder problems where information is missing or conflicting, and make decisions you can justify.

headingPath: Distinctive features of an Engineering degree

statements.about: lifecycle and resource impact
statements.paraphrase: Assessing the whole-life and environmental effects of engineering decisions is necessary for design in a world facing climate change; besides understanding low-carbon and clean technology, students should be able to assess the impact of exploiting resources.

forPractitioner.text: Teach lifecycle and environmental impact assessment alongside low-carbon and clean technologies, so students can judge the effects of resource exploitation.

forBeneficiary.text: You should be able to judge the environmental impact of engineering decisions over their whole life, including the effects of using up natural resources.

headingPath: Distinctive features of an Engineering degree

statements.about: cultural competence for a global sector
statements.paraphrase: UK engineering courses draw many international students and UK students can work worldwide and in international teams, so students should have the cultural competence to work in a global sector.

forPractitioner.text: Develop students' cultural competence for international teams and a global sector, drawing on the mix of UK and overseas students on the course.

forBeneficiary.text: You should build the cultural awareness and skills to work well in international teams and anywhere in the world.

headingPath: Distinctive features of an Engineering degree

statements.about: an inclusive course culture
statements.paraphrase: How courses are structured, delivered and assessed can strongly affect students, and inclusive education approaches help address this; an inclusive culture requires nurturing, constant re-evaluation and evidence, through student-centred design that values difference, design that fosters belonging and fair experience, chances to learn about every side of EDI, equity, justice and human rights among them, and EDI elements that support collaboration and self-reflection.

forPractitioner.text: Nurture an inclusive culture through student-centred course design that treats difference as a strength, design for belonging and equitable experience with accommodations, opportunities to learn about EDI including equity and justice, and EDI elements that support collaboration and reflection; keep re-evaluating it with evidence.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a requirement on the course culture; the student meets its effect

headingPath: Distinctive features of an Engineering degree

statements.about: progression through an honours degree
statements.paraphrase: Across a bachelor's degree at FHEQ Level 6 or FQHEIS Level 10, a student will move up level by level under institutional rules, each level adding knowledge, expertise and experience towards the threshold subject and generic skills; a graduate with a second-class degree or better would be expected to be ready for postgraduate study, though entry rules are set by each provider.

forPractitioner.text: Plan each level of the bachelor's degree so that it builds knowledge, expertise and experience towards the threshold subject-specific and generic skills; students will progress under institutional rules, and a graduate with a second or better would be expected to be ready for postgraduate study.

forBeneficiary.text: As you move through your degree, each year will build your knowledge, skills and experience towards the standard you need to graduate; with a second-class degree or better you would normally be ready for postgraduate study, though each university sets its own entry rules.

headingPath: Distinctive features of an Engineering degree

statements.about: progression through an integrated master's
statements.paraphrase: Across an integrated master's degree at FHEQ Level 7 or FQHEIS Level 11, a student will move up level by level under institutional rules, each year adding towards the threshold subject and generic skills; MEng progression rules are often stricter than BEng ones, so those who miss them may move to the matching bachelor's, and a graduate with a third or better would be expected to be ready for postgraduate study.

forPractitioner.text: Set progression requirements for the MEng (often stricter than for the BEng), plan each year to build towards the threshold-level skills, and provide a transfer route to the matching bachelor's for students who do not meet them.

forBeneficiary.text: On an integrated master's course you will move up year by year, building towards the standard you need to graduate; the rules for moving on are often stricter than on a bachelor's, and if you do not meet them you may transfer to the matching bachelor's degree.

headingPath: Distinctive features of an Engineering degree

statements.about: general and multidisciplinary degrees
statements.paraphrase: General and multidisciplinary honours degrees will reach the core subject and generic skills of engineering and will add others from the subjects in the joint course, and may explore where their subjects overlap.

forPractitioner.text: In a general or multidisciplinary honours degree, make sure students will achieve the core engineering subject and generic skills, then add the skills of the other subjects and use the overlap for interdisciplinary study.

forBeneficiary.text: On a general or joint engineering degree you will gain the core engineering skills plus skills from your other subject, with chances to work across both.

headingPath: Distinctive features of an Engineering degree

statements.about: accredited degree outcomes under AHEP
statements.paraphrase: A degree is awarded when a student shows they have met the course outcomes and the provider's award regulations; an accredited degree also needs the outcomes AHEP sets and any discipline requirements of the institution, so students on accredited courses are required to meet these harder requirements until an accredited award is no longer possible, after which the standard regulations apply.

forPractitioner.text: On an accredited course, apply AHEP's learning outcomes and the institution's extra requirements on top of the standard regulations, and switch to the standard regulations only once an accredited award is no longer possible for the student.

forBeneficiary.text: If your course is accredited, you must meet the extra, more demanding requirements set by the professional body as well as the usual ones; if you can no longer achieve an accredited degree, the usual university rules apply instead.

headingPath: Distinctive features of an Engineering degree

statements.about: keeping current through industry partnership
statements.paraphrase: Engineering courses sit in a fast-changing sector, so providers need to keep current with industry through active partnerships; industry advisory boards are essential to course design, offering insight into valued knowledge, skills and experience and into sector innovation.

forPractitioner.text: Keep the course current through active industry partnerships, using an industrial advisory board to advise on design, contemporary skill needs and sector innovation.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the provider; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

headingPath: Distinctive features of an Engineering degree

statements.about: community-centred design with EDI and ethics
statements.paraphrase: Engineering is in partnership with the society it serves; working with communities affected by engineering, and human- and community-centred design, can help students understand beneficiaries' needs, and such approaches should explicitly take EDI and ethical consequences into account.

forPractitioner.text: Use partnerships with affected community groups and human- and community-centred design to help students understand beneficiaries' needs, and make sure these approaches explicitly address EDI and ethics.

forBeneficiary.text: When you design for a community, you should work with the people affected and think explicitly about fairness, inclusion and ethics.

headingPath: Distinctive features of an Engineering degree

statements.about: external and industrial input to periodic review
statements.paraphrase: External input is a core part of UK quality assurance: providers will use external reviewers in periodic review to test proposed changes and confirm threshold standards and suitable content, and periodic review of engineering degrees should also bring in industrial partners to keep the curriculum current.

forPractitioner.text: In periodic review, use external reviewers to check threshold standards and content, and also draw on industrial partners so the curriculum stays current.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the provider in course review

statements.about: showing practical engineering ability
statements.paraphrase: Practical work matters especially because it sets engineering apart from other applied sciences; knowing in theory how to solve a problem is not enough, so the course needs to let learners show they can make a solution work in practice, from building and testing software to physical construction.

forPractitioner.text: Include opportunities for students to show they can make solutions work in practice, from build-and-test programming to build-and-test of physical constructions; theory alone is not enough.

forBeneficiary.text: Your course needs to give you chances to show that you can make engineering solutions work in practice, not just explain them in theory, whether that is software or a physical build.

statements.about: specialist content and fit with accreditation
statements.paraphrase: All engineering degrees leave providers room to add specialist content suited to their local and institutional setting; those seeking accreditation should make sure their outcomes match what the professional engineering institution and the Engineering Council require, and degrees can also include non-engineering subjects for breadth and choice.

forPractitioner.text: If seeking accreditation, check the learning outcomes against what the accrediting institution and the Engineering Council require; use the remaining flexibility for specialist and non-specialist content.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the provider seeking accreditation

statements.about: current curriculum; AHEP for accredited courses
statements.paraphrase: Curriculum design draws on current developments in research, scholarship and industrial practice and on where graduates may go; accredited courses must also meet AHEP's requirements.

forPractitioner.text: Inform the curriculum with current research, scholarship, industrial practice and graduate destinations; for accredited courses, meet AHEP's requirements as well.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a requirement on accredited courses

statements.about: lab work and projects on the bachelor's
statements.paraphrase: For a satisfactory understanding of engineering, bachelor's students are expected to have extensive practical laboratory work and sizeable projects, alone and in groups, including design, development and research projects that build independent thought and teamwork; teaching and learning needs to be set in social, ethical, legal, environmentally sustainable and economic contexts.

forPractitioner.text: On the bachelor's degree, give substantial hands-on lab work and individual and group projects (design, development and research) that develop independent thinking and effective teamwork, and set teaching in its social, ethical, legal, sustainable and economic context.

forBeneficiary.text: On a bachelor's course you can expect plenty of hands-on lab work and individual and group projects that build your independent thinking and teamwork, set in their social, ethical, legal, environmental and economic context.

statements.about: growing self-reliance on the master's
statements.paraphrase: Teaching on other master's courses, usually MSc, depends on the course's focus and may add specialism, breadth or depth; master's students are expected to become more self-reliant and self-directing, especially later in the course.

forPractitioner.text: Shape MSc teaching around the course's focus, and plan for students who will become steadily more self-reliant and self-directed, especially in the later stages.

forBeneficiary.text: On a taught master's course you will be expected to become more and more self-reliant and to direct your own learning, especially towards the end.

statements.about: designing for varied prior learning
statements.paraphrase: Many master's students took their first degree outside the UK system, and their earlier outcomes may not match UK graduates'; course design should allow for this.

forPractitioner.text: Design master's courses with students' varied prior learning in mind, since outcomes from first degrees outside the UK may not match UK ones.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on course design

statements.about: no award without achieved outcomes
statements.paraphrase: Following the qualifications frameworks, assessment procedures should not permit a qualification to be awarded where learning outcomes have not been met.

forPractitioner.text: Make sure assessment procedures cannot lead to an award when the learning outcomes have not been achieved.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on assessment procedures

statements.about: showing the output standards of the award
statements.paraphrase: Every engineering graduate will be able to show they have reached the output standards for the degree they hold; the provider publishes course aims and outcomes and sets sound assessment standards and procedures to check them.

forPractitioner.text: Publish course objectives and outcomes and set robust assessment standards and procedures so that every graduate will be able to show they have met the output standards for their award.

forBeneficiary.text: When you graduate, you will be able to show that you have met the standards for your degree; your course publishes its outcomes and assesses you against them.

statements.about: accessible assessment and reasonable adjustments
statements.paraphrase: Assessment centres on learning, lets students show their full theoretical and practical ability, aligns with outcomes and favours deep learning; providers offer accessible assessment methods and should also adjust reasonably for disabled students.

forPractitioner.text: Offer assessment methods accessible to all students and make reasonable adjustments for disabled students; align every assessment to outcomes and let students show theoretical and practical abilities.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the provider; the student receives the adjustments

statements.about: diverse and innovative assessment
statements.paraphrase: A variety of innovative assessment is encouraged, in person or remotely through digital technology; flexible assessment can widen access, and going beyond traditional exams lets students show different strengths, through methods such as exams, lab and project reports, case studies, literature reviews, dissertations, presentations, peer and self-assessment and work-integrated tasks.

forPractitioner.text: Use a diverse mix of innovative assessments, on site or remote, going beyond traditional exams so students can show varied strengths; the issuer encourages this rather than requiring it.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: guidance to those who design assessment

statements.about: criteria, feedback and academic integrity
statements.paraphrase: Each assessment's aims and requirements should be made clear through transparent marking criteria, with timely and useful feedback for every student; assessment should aim at the highest standards while closing off academic misconduct such as plagiarism and contract cheating, and published integrity policies should be actively promoted and consistently applied.

forPractitioner.text: Define each assessment's aims and requirements through transparent criteria, give all students timely feedback, design out plagiarism and contract cheating, and promote and apply integrity policies consistently.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on assessment design; the student meets its effect in criteria and feedback

statements.about: fair assessment of group work
statements.paraphrase: Students should have chances to show their skills through group work as well as individual assessment; fair assessment of group work underpins an inclusive curriculum, so the ability to work in a group, including inclusive behaviour and regard for differing abilities and styles, should be assessed, not just the output, alongside peer assessment and individual reflection on teamwork.

forPractitioner.text: Assess group work fairly: give students opportunities to show their skills in groups, assess how they work in the group (including inclusive behaviour) as well as the output, and use peer assessment and individual reflection.

forBeneficiary.text: You should get chances to show your skills in group work as well as alone, and expect to be assessed on how you work with others and to reflect on your own part.

statements.about: authentic assessment for employment
statements.paraphrase: Authentic assessment, which prepares students for work, is encouraged by attending to how students communicate, how technical skills are assessed and cultural competence.

forPractitioner.text: Use authentic assessment that reflects workplace communication, technical skills and cultural competence; the issuer encourages this.

forBeneficiary.text: Some of your assessments may look like real engineering work, testing how you communicate, your technical skills and how you work across cultures.

statements.about: strict limits on failure for accredited degrees
statements.paraphrase: Accredited degrees impose strict limits on failure and marginal failure, tighter than most providers' usual credit rules; students will usually have to pass most, sometimes all, modules to gain an accredited degree.

forPractitioner.text: On accredited degrees, apply the stricter limits on failure and marginal failure; students will typically need to pass most or all modules for the accredited award.

forBeneficiary.text: On an accredited course you will usually have to pass most, and sometimes all, of your modules to get the accredited degree; the rules are stricter than on many other courses.

statements.about: standards set against framework levels; accredited outcomes apply
statements.paraphrase: The standards are set against the relevant FHEQ Level 6 or 7 (FQHEIS 10 or 11) descriptors, so applying them to a course depends on context; many degrees are accredited by institutions licensed by the Engineering Council, and for accredited degrees the profession's outcomes for registration competences will apply.

forPractitioner.text: Read the standards against the FHEQ Level 6 or 7 descriptor for the award and apply them in context; for accredited degrees, the profession's learning outcomes will apply as well.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a statement for course designers on how the standards apply

statements.about: AHEP outcomes as the threshold for accredited courses
statements.paraphrase: For this text, the learning outcomes in the current edition of AHEP should be taken as the minimum threshold for accredited courses and read with the UK-SPEC statements of competence and commitment for Incorporated and Chartered Engineers.

forPractitioner.text: For accredited courses, treat AHEP's learning outcomes as the minimum threshold, reading them with UK-SPEC's competence and commitment statements for IEng and CEng.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a rule for course designers on accredited courses

statements.appliesTo: BEng with honours graduates at threshold
statements.about: coherent discipline knowledge and its application
statements.paraphrase: Will have shown joined-up knowledge and understanding of their branch of engineering and how it is put into practice.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, BEng graduates will have shown well-connected knowledge and understanding of their discipline and its use in practice.

forBeneficiary.text: To reach the minimum standard for a BEng with honours, you will have shown a joined-up understanding of your branch of engineering and how it is used in practice.

statements.appliesTo: BEng with honours graduates at threshold
statements.about: complex problems and safe, secure, sustainable solutions
statements.paraphrase: Will have shown they can recognise complex engineering problems, choose fitting tools and go on to produce safe, secure and sustainable solutions that meet set needs.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, BEng graduates will have shown they can identify complex engineering problems, pick suitable tools and produce safe, secure and sustainable answers to defined needs.

forBeneficiary.text: To reach the minimum standard for a BEng with honours, you will have shown that you can spot complex engineering problems, pick the right tools and create solutions that are safe, secure and sustainable and meet the need.

statements.appliesTo: BEng with honours graduates at threshold
statements.about: quantitative and computational analysis and its limits
statements.paraphrase: Will have shown the skill to choose and use quantitative and computational methods of analysis while knowing where those methods fall short.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, BEng graduates will have shown they can choose and use quantitative and computational analysis, aware of the limits of the methods.

forBeneficiary.text: To reach the minimum standard for a BEng with honours, you will have shown that you can choose and use numerical and computer-based analysis, and know where those methods stop being reliable.

statements.appliesTo: BEng with honours graduates at threshold
statements.about: creativity, innovation, teamwork and communication
statements.paraphrase: Will have shown creativity, innovation, teamwork and communication in carrying out engineering work.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, BEng graduates will have shown creativity, innovation, teamwork and communication in delivering engineering work.

forBeneficiary.text: To reach the minimum standard for a BEng with honours, you will have shown creativity and fresh thinking, worked well in a team and communicated clearly.

statements.appliesTo: BEng with honours graduates at threshold
statements.about: professional and commercial practice, ethics and global responsibility
statements.paraphrase: Will have shown that they value professional and commercial practice in engineering, ethics and social responsibility at a global scale.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, BEng graduates will have shown they appreciate how engineering is practised professionally and commercially, its ethics and its social responsibility worldwide.

forBeneficiary.text: To reach the minimum standard for a BEng with honours, you will have shown that you understand how engineering works as a profession and a business, and its ethical and social responsibilities around the world.

statements.appliesTo: BEng with honours graduates at the typical level
statements.about: typical level (2:1 and 2:2) set by marking schemes
statements.paraphrase: Criteria for the typical level, upper and lower second-class, will follow each provider's own undergraduate marking scheme and the sector-recognised standards used in each UK nation.

forPractitioner.text: Set 2:1 and 2:2 criteria from your institution's common or generic undergraduate marking scheme and your nation's sector-recognised standards; no subject-specific typical outcomes are given.

forBeneficiary.text: For a 2:1 or 2:2, you will be judged against your university's own marking scheme for undergraduate work and the national standards that apply where you study.

statements.appliesTo: BEng with honours graduates at the excellent level
statements.about: excellent level (first class) set by marking schemes
statements.paraphrase: Criteria for the excellent level, first-class, will follow each provider's own undergraduate marking scheme and the sector-recognised standards used in each UK nation.

forPractitioner.text: Set first-class criteria from your institution's common or generic undergraduate marking scheme and your nation's sector-recognised standards; no subject-specific excellent outcomes are given.

forBeneficiary.text: For a first, you will be judged against your university's own marking scheme for undergraduate work and the national standards that apply where you study.

statements.about: broad, coherent discipline knowledge and its application
statements.paraphrase: Will have shown broad, joined-up knowledge and understanding of their branch of engineering and how it is put into practice.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, MEng graduates will have shown wide and well-connected knowledge and understanding of their discipline and its use in practice.

forBeneficiary.text: To reach the minimum standard for an MEng, you will have shown a broad and joined-up understanding of your branch of engineering and how it is used in practice.

statements.about: complex problems and safe, secure, sustainable solutions
statements.paraphrase: Will have shown they can recognise complex engineering problems, choose fitting tools and go on to produce safe, secure and sustainable solutions that meet set needs.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, MEng graduates will have shown they can identify complex engineering problems, pick suitable tools and produce safe, secure and sustainable answers to defined needs.

forBeneficiary.text: To reach the minimum standard for an MEng, you will have shown that you can spot complex engineering problems, pick the right tools and create solutions that are safe, secure and sustainable and meet the need.

statements.about: analysis with incomplete data and its limits
statements.paraphrase: Will have shown the skill to choose and use quantitative and computational methods of analysis when data are incomplete, and to discuss where those methods fall short.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, MEng graduates will have shown they can choose and use quantitative and computational analysis with incomplete data and discuss the limits of the methods.

forBeneficiary.text: To reach the minimum standard for an MEng, you will have shown that you can choose and use numerical and computer-based analysis even when some data are missing, and explain the limits of your methods.

statements.about: creativity, innovation, effective teamwork, leadership and communication
statements.paraphrase: Will have shown creativity, innovation, effective teamwork, leadership and communication in carrying out engineering work.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, MEng graduates will have shown creativity, innovation, effective teamwork, leadership and communication in delivering engineering work.

forBeneficiary.text: To reach the minimum standard for an MEng, you will have shown creativity and fresh thinking, worked effectively in a team, taken a lead and communicated clearly.

statements.about: professional and commercial practice, ethics and global responsibility
statements.paraphrase: Will have shown that they value professional and commercial practice in engineering, ethics and social responsibility at a global scale.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, MEng graduates will have shown they appreciate how engineering is practised professionally and commercially, its ethics and its social responsibility worldwide.

forBeneficiary.text: To reach the minimum standard for an MEng, you will have shown that you understand how engineering works as a profession and a business, and its ethical and social responsibilities around the world.

statements.appliesTo: MEng graduates at the typical level
statements.about: typical level (2:1 and 2:2) set by marking schemes
statements.paraphrase: Criteria for the typical level, upper and lower second-class, will follow each provider's own marking scheme for integrated master's courses.

forPractitioner.text: Set 2:1 and 2:2 criteria for the MEng from your institution's common or generic integrated master's marking scheme; no subject-specific typical outcomes are given.

forBeneficiary.text: For a 2:1 or 2:2 on an integrated master's, you will be judged against your university's own marking scheme for these courses.

statements.appliesTo: MEng graduates at the excellent level
statements.about: excellent level (first class) set by marking schemes
statements.paraphrase: Criteria for the excellent level, first-class, will follow each provider's own marking scheme for integrated master's courses.

forPractitioner.text: Set first-class criteria for the MEng from your institution's common or generic integrated master's marking scheme; no subject-specific excellent outcomes are given.

forBeneficiary.text: For a first on an integrated master's, you will be judged against your university's own marking scheme for these courses.

statements.about: threshold in every category for the MSc
statements.paraphrase: Postgraduate master's graduates must show at least threshold attainment in every relevant outcome category, usually equivalent to a pass.

forPractitioner.text: Make sure every MSc graduate shows at least threshold attainment across all relevant outcome categories; threshold usually matches a pass.

forBeneficiary.text: To get a taught master's in engineering you must reach at least the minimum standard in every relevant area of the course; that usually means a pass.

statements.about: coherent knowledge of the discipline or specialism
statements.paraphrase: Will have shown joined-up knowledge and understanding of their branch of engineering or their specialism.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, MSc graduates will have shown well-connected knowledge and understanding of their discipline or specialism.

forBeneficiary.text: To reach the minimum standard for a taught MSc, you will have shown a joined-up understanding of your branch of engineering or your specialist area.

statements.about: complex problems and safe, secure, sustainable solutions
statements.paraphrase: Will have shown they can recognise complex engineering problems, choose fitting tools and go on to produce safe, secure and sustainable solutions that meet set needs.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, MSc graduates will have shown they can identify complex engineering problems, pick suitable tools and produce safe, secure and sustainable answers to defined needs.

forBeneficiary.text: To reach the minimum standard for a taught MSc, you will have shown that you can spot complex engineering problems, pick the right tools and create solutions that are safe, secure and sustainable and meet the need.

statements.about: analysis with incomplete data and its limits
statements.paraphrase: Will have shown the skill to choose and use quantitative and computational methods of analysis when data are incomplete, and to discuss where those methods fall short.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, MSc graduates will have shown they can choose and use quantitative and computational analysis with incomplete data and discuss the limits of the methods.

forBeneficiary.text: To reach the minimum standard for a taught MSc, you will have shown that you can choose and use numerical and computer-based analysis even when some data are missing, and explain the limits of your methods.

statements.about: creativity, innovation, research, effective teamwork, leadership and communication
statements.paraphrase: Will have shown creativity, innovation, research, effective teamwork, leadership and communication in carrying out engineering work.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, MSc graduates will have shown creativity, innovation, research, effective teamwork, leadership and communication in delivering engineering work.

forBeneficiary.text: To reach the minimum standard for a taught MSc, you will have shown creativity and fresh thinking, carried out research, worked effectively in a team, taken a lead and communicated clearly.

statements.about: professional and commercial practice, ethics and global responsibility
statements.paraphrase: Will have shown that they value professional and commercial practice in engineering, ethics and social responsibility at a global scale.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, MSc graduates will have shown they appreciate how engineering is practised professionally and commercially, its ethics and its social responsibility worldwide.

forBeneficiary.text: To reach the minimum standard for a taught MSc, you will have shown that you understand how engineering works as a profession and a business, and its ethical and social responsibilities around the world.
